# University of Edinburgh Summary
The University of Edinburgh has a rich history, originating from an endowment by Bishop Robert Reid in 1557. It received a royal charter in 1582, opening in 1583. During the 18th century, it was a central location of the Scottish Enlightenment, attracting key figures such as Adam Smith and David Hume. The university gained full authority over its own affairs in 1858 under the Universities (Scotland) Act. Key institutional developments include the founding of the Edinburgh University Union (EUU) in 1889, which merged to form the current Edinburgh University Students' Association (EUSA) in 1973.
The university operates across several main sites, including the Central Area (home to the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences and the School of Informatics), King's Buildings (where much of the Science and Engineering College's activities take place), the BioQuarter, Easter Bush, and Western General. It comprises three Colleges: Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, Science & Engineering, and Medicine & Vet Medicine. Notable sub-units include the Roslin Institute, which gained international recognition for cloning Dolly the sheep. The University of Edinburgh is a member of the Russell Group and is known for its numerous academic and scientific contributions.
